Made by and Forwarded by

With reference to the memos of the Officer i/c Special
Branch dated June 16 and 20, 1933, relating to a statement of
Hsia Tsai Hsi(夏希希) alias Tsing Gee(清奇) alias Tsai Gee
(蔡奇) alias Li Chie-chen(李菊村), bearing on "The No. 7
Quinsan Garden's case", which was published in the "Shanghai
Evening Post & Mercury" of June 15 and in the "China Forum" of
June 19, 1933, I have to state that enquiries have been made by
the undersigned in conjunction with detectives from Louza Station
at the Great Shanghai Hotel, No. 348 Tientsin Road, with the
following results:-

Between 9 a.m. and 9.30 a.m., May 9, 1933, Li Chie-chen
(李菊村), who had a large handbag in his possession, booked room
No. 220 on the second floor. He paid the rent himself and
remained alone in the room until May 10 when he left.
The following particulars regarding this individual are inscribed
in the hotel guest book:-
"Li Chu Ling(李菊林), aged 28, native of Shanghai,
"merchant by profession. Came to hotel on May 9 and
"departed on May 10. "

The difference in name is evidently a clerical error made by the
hotel accountant as the Chinese characters Ling(林) and chen
(村) only differ very slightly.

Immediately after Li Chie-chen had registered, a stoutly
built person giving the name of Loh Ts Lan(陸子樓) came to the
hotel. (His nickname Wu-sze鬍子是 mentioned in the statement
of Li Chie-chen as published in the press). He desired to
book room No. 222 which is directly opposite room No. 220
occupied by Li, but as that room was then occupied by others,
he finally took room No. 219. The particulars contained in

Having settled down in room 219 at 9.45 a.m. May 9, Loh

the telephone, Loh Ts Leu was overheard by hotel 'boy' No. 39
named Zien Ah Kung(錢阿根), calling himself by the name Wu-sze.
Shortly afterwards four or five persons, some wearing short
clothing and others longgowns, visited Loh in room 219. Loh and
his visitors then commenced playing Mah Jong in the room with the
door left open, at the same time taking turns in keeping a
vigilant watch on the movements of Li Chie-chen, the occupant of
room No. 220.
The action on the part of the occupants of room No. 219
subsequently aroused the suspicions of 'boy' No. 39 who then
asked Li Chie-chen whether he had had any trouble with the men
in room No. 219. Li Chie-chen replied that he was aware of
the watch being kept on him and that he was afraid that his life
was in danger. He requested the 'boy' not to report the
matter to the hotel management and entreated the 'boy' to help
him to escape during the night of May 10. He further promised
to reward the 'boy' after he had got out of danger, but he refused
to mention where he intended to go. He also stated that he
was engaged in the sundry goods business and that he was

The occupant of room 220, upon being interviewed, denied
having told the boy to fetch the Police. This individual
was advised that if he wished to leave the premises whilst the

According to the record kept by the hotel, Loh Ts Leu
alias Wu-sze sent out a second telephone message from his room

and had an altercation with 'boy' No. 30 regarding the report

'Boy' No. 30, when shown a photograph of Ma Shao Wu,
could not identify him as being the visitor, although information
from other sources indicates that the visitor was none other than
Ma Shao Wu.
Li Chie-chen vacated room No. 220 shortly after the
Police visit and left by the back door. He was immediately
followed by the occupants of room No. 219 who also left by the
back door. Nobody in the hotel observed in which direction
they went.
When renting the rooms Li Chie-chen and Loh Ts Leu alias
Wu-sze filled in registration forms in duplicate, one copy
being sent to the accountant's office for entry into the guest
book, the other being kept by the 'boys' on duty for purposes
of reference. However, the forms in question cannot now
be traced because all such forms for May and previous months,
according to the accountant Zah Wen Foo(石文甫), have been
destroyed for the reason that they were useless, the particulars
contained therein having already been recorded in the register.
Moreover, as numerous forms are used daily it would be inadvisable
to keep the forms for longer than about one month since they
accumulate too quickly.

The above statement is further corroborated by
information obtained from the Chinese authorities through Supt.
Tan Shao Liang to the effect that room No. 219 was occupied by
Ma Shao Wu, late Nanking Political Agent, and four of his agents,
while Li Chie-chen, the occupant of room No. 220, was an informer
engaged by Ma and had rented the room with the object of keeping
an appointment with an alleged communist suspect. (Vide attached
report of May 15).

Twelve copies of the photograph of Hsia Tsai Hsi were

Upon being shown the photograph, 'boys' Nos. 30 and 39,
who served rooms 219 and 220 in the Great Shanghai Hotel, were
unable to say definitely whether the man in the photograph was
Li Chie-chen who occupied room No. 220 on May 9-10. They
admitted that, apart from the face being fatter, the man in the
photograph resembled Li Chie-chen who also wore glasses.
However, the hotel detective Woo Ching Ping(吴金斌) is positive
that the occupant of room 220, Li Chie-chen, was identical with
the original of the photo.

On June 23, the photograph of Hsia was shown by D.S.
Tilton to Mrs. S. Levy, proprietress of the boarding house at
No. 7 Quinsan Gardens. She is of the opinion that the
photo strongly resembles one of the visitors who came to her
establishment on May 14 and who spoke to her in English that
'they knew the way', meaning the room occupied by Ting Ling and
Mann Fung.

Hsia Tsai Hsi(夏采希), aged 33, native of Huangtu,
medium build, smart appearance, parted hair, wearing gold rimmed
glasses. He was formerly engaged in special work of the
Chinese Communist Party. He was arrested by the Chinese
authorities at the Peiping Railway Station on or about April 23,
1933, for being an active communist on information given by one
Wong Yuen Zung(王雲程), a converted communist, who was then
travelling en route from Tientsin to Peiping. On the day
following his arrest he was escorted to Nanking where he showed
signs of repentance and signed a surrender form to the Nanking
authorities. After staying at Nanking for a few days he
was transferred to Shanghai to work under the late Ma Shao Wu.
Here he gradually won Ma's confidence and after acting as an
agent for Ma for a period of 10-14 days he suddenly disappeared
on May 14. This caused Ma to feel extremely uneasy and
he ordered all his offices to be removed. Ma also dispatched
an urgent message to this effect to Nanking the same evening
(May 14) through the long distance telephone requesting among
other matters that the photograph of Hsia be sent to Shanghai
for reproduction purposes. Hsia was a graduate of the
Nanyang College and possessed a good knowledge of English and
Chinese. He acted as Chief of the Second Section of the
Special Administration Department of the Chinese Communist Party
during the period when Koo Cheng Chang(顾顺章) was the Head of
that department.

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Thursday, June 15, 1933

Car Number Links
Sing Song Murder
To Girl Kidnapping

License Plate 4223 On Official Bureau Of Public
Safety Auto Discovered Same As One Used
During Disappearance Of Ting Ling

NANKING SENDS INVESTIGATOR

A motorcar license plate bearing the number 4223 has furnished evidence linking last night's murder of Ma Shou-wu, Central Kuomintang Headquarters agent attached to the Bureau of Public Safety in the largely honorary capacity of inspector, with the Settlement kidnapping on May 14 of Miss Ting Ling, girl writer, and Pan Chu-nien and the death of Ting Chiu.

Ma was shot dead by four unidentified men just after he had alighted from a car bearing license plate 4223—an official Bureau car detailed to his use—at Chekiang Road and Lane 229, near Foochow Road. He was about to dine in a sing-song house known as "Sweetheart."

Identical Plates

An article to be published by the China Forum magazine next Monday, signed by Li Chie-chen who is described as a witness to the May 14 kidnapping, says that the car in which Ting Ling and Pan were abducted bore license plate 4223.

This information came as no surprise to unofficial investigators of the May 14 affair, it was learned today. Further than this, however, no one was prepared to be quoted at the present stage of the inquiry.

Under Nanking Orders

Ma is understood to have operated entirely under instructions from Nanking. Local authorities collaborated with and assisted him in his activities against political subjects but he was subjected to no routine duties under their orders. He had returned from Nanking only yesterday, having left Shanghai for Nanking immediately following the publication of the Ting Ling kidnapping story in The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury.

Last night's shooting occurred about 9 o'clock from the home of a girl who was Ma's frequent companion. He had planned supper with her and several others, and eventually his guests arrived at the house in a car which stopped him in the alleyway from which they opened heavy fire, bringing Ma down before he could draw his service pistol.

Found By Chauffeur

Sing-song girls of the neighborhood, and Ma's chauffeur who came after him on foot to collect his "supper tip," found Ma lying in a pool of blood with one bullet near the ear, one in the jaw, one through the temple and a fourth through the chest. He died 10 minutes later at the Lester Chinese hospital.

Police investigation is under way. The only result available today was establishment of the fact that the shooting was carefully calculated and apparently staged by persons intimately familiar with Ma's personal life and after careful surveillance.

It was revealed that a search of Ma's garments at the hospital had disclosed a notebook giving names of communist suspects throughout the Shanghai area.

China Forum Account

The China Forum story on the May 14 affair, by a person not in touch with the authorities, is understood in certain of its aspects to correspond with unconfirmed information already obtained by investigating officials.

The Li story conflicts with the position taken by Settlement police in its allegations of police collaboration with Ma and his men. It is pointed out that action on behalf of the Chinese authorities has been taken only when they had obtained official authority from the Special District Court, and that no person was transferred outside the jurisdiction of the Settlement until a prima facie case to the satisfaction of the Municipal Advocate's office had been made out.

Story Of Li

Factual portions of the Li story follow:

"I witnessed the kidnapping of Ting Ling and Pan Chu-nien and the murder of Ting Chiu who was also known as Ting Hsu-jen. I witnessed the treatment of other victims of kidnapping and torture in the Shanghai hotel in which I was kept prisoner.

"But I succeeded in escaping from my brutal captors after being in their hands for two weeks. I escaped from them while they were kidnapping Ting Ling and Pan and I know they haven't left a single stone unturned anywhere to get their hands on me again. They have taken vengeance upon me by seizing my brothers and sister and even my 80-year-old mother! But I have again come to North China to join in the Volunteer front fighting against Japanese imperialism and its Kuomintang lackeys. I consider it my imperative duty to reveal what I underwent during the period of my detention and to disclose in detail the character of the Kuomintang regime, appealing against it to the toiling masses of the whole country."

in a motorcar with the License No. 4223. Later I learned that their names were Ma Chao-wu alias Lu Ka-ching and Hsu Wei-san alias Yen Koh-cing. These men are the ring-leaders of Shanghai's gangster detectives. Ma holds rank as an Inspector in the Bureau of Public Safety. He holds power in that capacity to order any arrest he pleases and works in close cooperation with the Shanghai Municipal Police.

Drive Across City

"The motorcar in which I was taken drove across the city along Honan Road to the East Gate where we drew up in front of the Best Hun-chi Hotel. I was placed in Room 25 on the second floor. My captors seemed to be well-known to the waiters and other hotel attendants. Later I knew this was because they always brought their kidnapped victims to this place which was used both as headquarters and prison.

"Here I was to be kept under heavy guard. There were at least 20 men who took turns guarding my room. Gradually I came to know a considerable number of them. One of them is a completely degenerate scoundrel, a giant of a man about 40 years old named Lee Ching-hu. Another, about 20 years old, was nicknamed Wu-sze because he was so hairy. His real name was Chung and he was very strong. These two men were the main operatives in the kidnapping game. Each time Lee would pose as a police detective. Wu-sze did the strong-arm work of actually carrying out the forcible capture.

"High-nose" Kidnapper

"There was another man named Pei Sou-kan who was called "High-nose" or O-moh by his fellow-gangsters. This one would boast that he has carried out kidnappings in the open street! He was formerly in prison as a criminal but was brought out and especially paid by Ma Chao-wu to do this work. There were also many others, Ting Tze-yi, Ho Shih-shing, Shen Seng-ting, Chou Kwang-yah and many whose names I never did learn. Most of their prisoners they would hand over to the Bureau of Public Safety.

"Inspector Ma and Hsu Wei-san demanded that I lead them to the home of those I knew to be engaged in anti-imperialist activities. This was why I was brought to Shanghai. I refused to do so. But then I decided to maneuver for time and for a chance to escape. I wrote a post-card addressed to a non-existent person asking 'somebody' to meet me at the Best Hun-chi Hotel on Chekiang Road, the International Settlement, on the night of May 9-10. I signed the same signature I am using here—Li Chie-chen. I showed my captors what I had written and they were very pleased. On May 9 I was taken to this hotel and placed in Room 25 on the second floor.

Escape Impossible
"Wu-sze occupied Room 19 next to mine. There were at least six or seven others who either stayed in my room or sauntered up and down the hall outside. I wracked my brains for a way to escape but soon had to realize it was impossible. There are too many of them around the hotel. I was alone in my room during the night and until the early morning I watched the window of Room 19, where a light still shone. Finally it went out at 3 o'clock.
"I opened my own window as softly as I could, planning to get down somehow to the alleyway which led directly to Nanking Road. A hotel watchman was sweeping the alley. I closed my window and waited. A few minutes later I opened the window again. The watchman was gone but creeping along the ledge of the floor below were two thieves trying to force an entry into the place! I didn't dare climb out. It would have meant parleying with the thieves and this would certainly have awakened the men in No. 19. As a matter of fact at that moment the window of No. 19 did open. I slipped back, sick at heart. It was already dawn.
"Took Another Chance"
"Next morning I took another long chance. The waiters and boys in the hotel suspected the character of my captors. I begged one to provide me with soft slippers and an opportunity to escape. He immediately reported to the police. A squad of seven men of the Shanghai Municipal Police came to the hotel that same morning to inquire. When my captors informed them they were Ma Chao-wu's men, the policemen left. All hope of escape left me. I was brought back on the morning of May 11 to the East Hun-Chi Hotel.

"At 9 o'clock the morning of May 12 a group of these detectives, Ho Shih-sing, Yu Shih-shen, Woo Min-tung and Ting Chi-wen brought a man, a woman and a child to the hotel. They had been picked up off the street. This man was accused of being a Communist although they had no evidence to prove it, and right there in the hotel he was severely beaten on the head and face by one of the gangsters, Cheng Kwong-yin of the Bureau of Public Safety. The prisoner later in the day was sent to the Bureau. His wife and child were kept in Room No. 30 of the hotel.
Another Kidnap Victim
"The afternoon of that same day, the 12th, another man was brought to the hotel. He had also been kidnapped on the streets. On May 13 four persons were likewise seized and brought to the hotel. Two of them were man and wife who had just arrived in Shanghai to go to school here. They were imprisoned in a small room just back of No. 30. There they were thrown to the floor and beaten with bamboo carrying poles. I heard the beating.
"Thus these men passed from day to day, like beasts of prey. They would never read newspapers or books, of which they knew nothing. It was only their job to kidnap revolutionaries. The rest of the time they spent gorging themselves with food and drink, gambling, sleeping with prostitutes and taking salvarsan injections. All of them professional thugs and gangsters paid agents of the Kuomintang.
Inspector Arrives
"On May 14 Inspector Ma, accompanied by Hsu Wei-san and Chong Kwong-yin came to the hotel. I heard him say: We have discovered that Ting Ling lives in Room No. 2 on the fourth floor of House No. 7, Quinsan Road. She is a counter-revolutionary and this afternoon Pan Chu-nien and Ting Chiu—(Ying Shu-jen—ED) will visit her this afternoon." Ma ordered that I come along to identify them. One of the detectives named Chu Kwong-yah said he knew them and could also identify them. Inspector Ma immediately designated six men, including himself, to make the trip.
"At one o'clock I was bundled into a motorcar with them. It was the same car which had originally brought me from North Station—license No. 4223. Our car was parked on Pierce Road and in a group we entered House No. 7 in Quinsan Gardens. Inspector Ma was dressed in foreign clothes, a gray suit, and carried a leather portfolio with him in one hand and a revolver in the other. Thus he stood when he knocked on the door.
Ting Ling Opens Door
"A girl—Ting Ling—opened the door. Her face blanched but nothing was said. Pan was sitting in the room. Inspector Ma immediately searched Pan's clothes and then in foul language ordered them both to come with him. Pan, short of stature, his brown face looking somehow aged, remained calm, a half-smile crossing his countenance.
The gangsters stood crowded around the door. Miss Ting put on a coat and hastily bundled up some extra clothes. Ma and two others took them away. Chong Kwong-yin, who I also learned holds rank as Inspector, in the Bureau of Public Safety, three other gangster-detectives and myself were ordered to remain in the room.
"They began to tear up the room, searching for documents. They found nothing but well-known magazines and books. Chong growled. 'Anyway, they're reactionaries. Their writing is sympathetic to the Communist movement. We sat there in the room and waited. My throat and mouth were dry. Yet I felt so helpless.
Knock On Door
"Shortly before four o'clock, there was a knock on the door. A tall man, wearing a gray long gown and glasses walked in. He was Ying Hsu-jen, who is also known as Ting Chiu. His expression immediately underwent a change as the situation in the room presented itself to him. He was seized and Chong immediately began searching him.
"Ying resisted and started a fight with Chong. The other detectives came to Chong's aid. Chou Kwong-ya remained at my side and I immediately attacked him. I saw Ying fighting with his back against the window, the three men striking at him savagely. I had my own hands full with Chou. I heard a shout and looked up. Ying was gone! The window stood wide open. It faced on an alleyway leading to Haining Road. When this happened Chong and the others rushed out of the door.
Run For Freedom
"A minute later I had pinned Chou to the floor and stunned him with a blow full in the face. I scrambled up and dashed out of the door, slamming it behind me. I ran breathlessly down the stairs. Room No. 2 faced to the back and the others were there. I ran out of the front door and out in the street became once more a free man.
"Next morning I read in the papers of the dead man found in Quinsan Road. He had been murdered!"

With reference to the attached questionnaire of the
Officer i/c Special Branch, I have to report that D.I. Kuh Pao-
hwa and the undersigned visited the Great Shanghai Hotel, 348
Tientsin Road, and ascertained from the hotel manager that on
May 9, 1933 room 220 was booked by a male Chinese who gave his
name as Li Chu Ling (李菊林), while the adjoining room, No.219,
was taken a few minutes later by one Loh Ts Leu (陆子楼) who
was afterwards joined by five others. The occupant of room 220
complained on May 11 to the hotel detective that his movements
were being watched by the people in room 219. The hotel detective
reported the matter to Louza Station and a party of detectives
proceeded to the hotel in question and found that room 219 was
being used by the subordinates of Liu Kuh Ching (刘谷青), Nanking
Political Agent, for the purpose of keeping observation on
communist suspects. No other visit was paid to this hotel by
the Police.
On the morning of May 13 the supposed suspect in room
220 left the hotel and 15 minutes later the party occupying room
